\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:7}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{7}

This thesis examined the association between water and sanitation conditions and the anthropometric outcomes of children in four Sub-Saharan African countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria. Two distinctions ran through the analysis: between a child's own household facilities and the WASH conditions of the surrounding community, and between a single exposure measured at the survey date and a preliminary, geospatially matched measure of modelled local WASH coverage during the child's own early-life window, constructed for an earlier survey round in three of the four countries, with Ethiopia retained only as a provisional sensitivity analysis (Section 1.4).

The baseline evidence does not show a clear, robust association between improved household WASH and child anthropometric outcomes when households are compared within the same DHS cluster (Section 5.1); under this design, that is an inconclusive result, not evidence that no association exists. The community measure, estimated with region rather than cluster fixed effects for the reason given in Section 4.3, shows a large, significant association before adjustment for most outcome and exposure pairs, which attenuates to non-significance once socioeconomic status and region fixed effects are added (Section 5.2). This attenuation is consistent with confounding by local development, but the design cannot establish confounding as the only explanation. Both patterns are broadly consistent with the strongest available causal evidence: the three major WASH trials found no statistically detectable effect of basic, household-level interventions on linear growth, without the trial authors treating this as evidence against WASH's biological plausibility (Section 2.3) --- a suggestive, not confirmatory, parallel, since this thesis's exposure is a facility-type classification in survey data, not a randomised, comprehensive intervention package.

The historical extension links earlier DHS rounds from Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria to IHME's modelled annual local WASH coverage for a defined early-life window, an area average around displaced cluster coordinates that is neither observed historical household access nor population-weighted coverage (Sections 3.5, 6.5). Its selected headline cell, the pooled established-date association between local water coverage and height-for-age, is positive and significant, reconstructed independently with a second estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample (Appendix B) --- a check that confirms the computation, not the number of cells tested or the association's causal status, and not the only nominally significant historical cell (Section 5.6). The finding carries substantial qualifications set out in full in Section 6: sensitivity to the pooled weighting convention, a working inference in place of undocumented measurement-subsample weighting, exposure-source overlap with the DHS surveys it is compared against, current residence standing in for early-life residence, and within-cluster exposure variation far smaller than the reporting scale. The contrast with the baseline results cannot be attributed to exposure timing, because the two samples differ at once in children, survey rounds, exposure construction, eligibility rules and control sets (Section 6.2). This is a preliminary, qualified finding, not one that overturns or reinterprets the more cautious baseline conclusions.

Taken together, the thesis makes two separate contributions in two separate samples (Section 1.5): a side-by-side comparison of own-household and leave-one-out community WASH exposure within one four-country sample and one consistent control set, each estimated under the fixed-effects structure its construction requires; and, in the historical sample, a documented, preliminary attempt to introduce genuine temporal variation in early-life exposure through geospatially matched coverage data. Because the historical data cannot separate a child's own household from its community, the second contribution does not extend the household-versus-community comparison.

Neither set of results, alone or together, establishes a causal effect of WASH facilities on child nutritional outcomes in these four countries, which were selected for data availability and recency, not to represent Sub-Saharan Africa as a whole (Sections 1.4, 6.6). Nor can the results be read as evidence for or against the value of WASH investment as a development policy: weak or inconclusive nutritional associations in an associational, four-country design do not show that such investment lacks value, and no causal policy effect or cost-effectiveness was estimated. What the thesis offers instead is an account of where its evidence is stronger, where it is weaker, and where further data or a different design would be needed before a stronger claim could responsibly be made --- most clearly, the unresolved measurement documentation of the historical extension and the exposure-timing limitation inherent in the baseline design.

Future work could address these gaps directly. Validating the Ethiopian interview-date conversion would allow the historical approach to cover all four countries on an established-date basis (Appendix C). The measurement-subsample weighting question could be resolved through direct engagement with DHS methodological documentation. And geospatial WASH matching could be combined with a design that follows the same geographic units over successive survey rounds (Section 1.2) --- natural next steps toward narrowing the gap this thesis has described but not closed.
